So, with the 33 constituencies in the Eastern Region, the only two roads were allocated to the Minister’s Constituency. Mr Speaker, I find it hard to understand but as the Minister for Roads and Highways is here, he knows that there are a lot of roads that need to be considered. So, I still question the criteria for selecting those roads. Mr Speaker, I was also thinking about the fact that the Minister said that if GH₵13.8 billion is approved, the selected roads are going to be constructed, it is fine. We are still waiting to see if the values that will come will conform to the allocated budget. That is why we expect them to come back. Another thing is the District Road Improvement Programme (DRIP) because these roads are not enough for Members. 123 30th July, 2025 124 Multi-Year Commitments for Selected Road Projects Under Big Push Programme Members keep asking for roads because road issues have been the biggest challenge in this country. Every Member of Parliament is looking for roads in their constituency. Now we have the DRIP. The NPP government purchased those equipment to make roads motorable and I remember on the Committee where we had the Minister for Roads and Highways then as a Ranking Member, all he kept pushing was that “Minister, it is not about doing asphalt, it is about making the roads motorable. Now my question is that, how are we going to make all roads motorable? Because this “Big Push” cannot solve all the road issues in this country. The DRIP that we purchased—the DRIP that the NPP Government supplied materials and fuel, are now all being packed. We do not know when they are going to be put into use. So, our advice is that the Minister considers the usage of the DRIP to make most roads motorable. I think that was even going to be bigger than the “Big Push” because with the DRIP, every district had the equipment to do their own roads or make their roads motorable. Every district in Ghana had one; I do not think the “Big Push” is covering every district in Ghana. That is why I said, even in the Eastern Region where we have only two roads selected for the first phase, yet we have the DRIP. So, I will plead with the Minister to use the DRIP in fixing most of the roads in the country and also plead with him that there is a constituency called Kade where we also have roads to be constructed. So, in the second phase, he should try to consider the Kade to Asuom roads for me. He should also try to do the Otumi to Abirem roads for me. Thank you, Mr Speaker. In supporting this Motion, I should premise my support on three issues. One is the re- introduction of the road tolls; the second is the poor quality of our roads and the third one is the poor engineering of our roads. Mr Speaker, the Committee tells us that the road tolls are likely to be re- introduced. I believe that for good reason, the Government had the policy of not having tolls collected. At the time, we were receiving just a little over GH₵70 million. We are told that there was a research by a very respected organisation. This research revealed that over 70 per cent of tolls collected ended up in wrong hands. So, the records had a far lesser amount, and this was very insufficient. I hold the view that this re- introduction of the road tolls, which re- introduction my respected Colleague, the Hon Chief Whip on the Minority Bench has no problem with, upon being re- introduced, should come with a digitalised solution to sustain it so that the human interface will be minimised, if not eradicated. We have systems that would allow a perfect way of collecting these tolls for the funds to get into Government’s hands. I believe that with the work done by this research body that revealed that if the road tolls are properly accounted for, we are likely to rake in, between, GH₵2.5 and GH₵3 billion — If this is done with proper digitalisation, I believe that we can even get more. Mr Speaker, having said that, I have heard the lamentations of the Committee and that of Hon Colleagues who had the opportunity to speak before me. They talked about amounts owed contractors. It is true, but we as a political class are loud on moneys owed contractors. Yes, Hon Nyindam? According to the Reports, it has been one of the challenges that the previous Administration faced. Roads and transport infrastructure issues were discussed in Parliament, particularly regarding:

* Allocation of funds for road construction and maintenance [dff4571f96a0c9d7265906fba17679b935006ecfb10abc19742dff121af4c1f3:59]
* Poor quality of roads and the need for improvement [217f0c90ad02f0f71a5a8fd57ce4d2deb97070e6c3fc77f4be86456c6f3723c2:24]
* Delays in payment or execution of road projects, with institutions such as the Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of Roads and Highways being questioned [c5c72f37c302ef9b1452d16465c23ef330167c1b086da25efca6cdf9bd4bd0e3:10]
* The need for a fair distribution of national resources, including roads, to all constituencies [217f0c90ad02f0f71a5a8fd57ce4d2deb97070e6c3fc77f4be86456c6f3723c2:24]
* Flooding and connectivity issues on certain bridges, such as the one between Walewale and Nalerigu [217f0c90ad02f0f71a5a8fd57ce4d2deb97070e6c3fc77f4be86456c6f3723c2:24]
* The District Road Improvement Programme (DRIP) and the need for more roads to be constructed [dff4571f96a0c9d7265906fba17679b935006ecfb10abc19742dff121af4c1f3:59]
